source.title: Optimizing Deeper Transformers on Small Datasets
source.authors: Peng Xu; Dhruv Kumar; Wei Yang; Wenjie Zi; Keyi Tang; Chenyang Huang; J. Cheung; S. Prince; Yanshuai Cao

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Applies a data-dependent initialization method to newly added transformer layers in small-data NLP tasks and reports training and performance outcomes; this extends initialization/trainability findings to a pretrained-transformer setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation/test accuracy and explicit training convergence or failure, not training classification error. It does not test random-initialized networks from scratch, CIFAR benchmarks, or the specific normalization, shortcut, and width conditions in the versions. Rows capture reported initialization/depth outcomes relevant to V4; cited prior-work results are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study develops and evaluates DT-Fixup for residual transformer layers added above pretrained RoBERTa. It uses Xavier initialization and extends transformer Fixup, but does not test V4's activation-matched initialization in plain networks or its orthogonal-weight predictions. Layer normalization removal in transformers also does not test V6's batch-normalization or specified residual-network comparisons. Its initialization, convergence and depth findings therefore fit no supplied version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that DT-Fixup enables deeper transformers above pretrained encoders to train with faster convergence and improved generalization on small Spider and ReClor datasets. These conclusions concern their combined optimization strategy, rather than an isolated initialization intervention.
record.recipe_differences: Uses data-dependent DT-Fixup initialization for newly added transformers on pretrained encodings; removes warm-up and layer normalization in new layers. It does not use the random-initialization CIFAR classification recipes in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization strategy and number of added layers change reported training outcomes; standard optimization degrades at greater depth, while DT-Fixup supports deeper models. Dataset/task also changes the size of the reported benefit.

fits_no_version.finding: DT-Fixup improves downstream accuracy over standard optimization as added transformer depth increases. Table 5 reports successful DT-Fixup training up to 32 added layers on Spider and 16 on ReClor, whereas standard optimization performs poorly beyond 8.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-dependent initialization combined with removal of layer normalization and warm-up can enable deeper residual transformer stacks above pretrained encoders to train on small NLP datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying T-Fixup after dropping its input constraints fails to converge in 4 of 5 runs in the mixed pretrained/new-layer setup.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformer initialization schemes can fail when their assumptions about input scale are violated by pretrained encodings.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.3 and Figure 2 report faster attainment of comparable Spider validation performance with DT-Fixup, especially for deeper models; the supplied text does not provide numerical curve coordinates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DT-Fixup accelerates validation-performance convergence for added transformer layers above pretrained encoders on Spider.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study uses pretrained RoBERTa encodings and measures downstream accuracy rather than training classification error. The main Spider and ReClor results do not test random initialization of the entire network. The text reports means and standard deviations for ablations but not all run-level results.
record.rows_left_out: Rows for standard and DT-Fixup at Spider 16 and 24 layers and ReClor 4, 8, and 16 layers are included. No otherwise qualifying reported training outcomes were omitted.

untested.parts: Training classification error in randomly initialized convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including random or corrupted labels and the specified capacity and training-recipe conditions.
Spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks versus identity-shortcut networks; the specified plain tanh and normalization-free residual alternatives.

Activation-matched initialization and signal or gradient propagation in plain networks; orthogonal versus equal-variance Gaussian initialization in deep tanh networks; orthogonal convolution kernels at extreme depth. Added transformer blocks retain skip connections, and DT-Fixup also changes normalization and warm-up.
Loss recovery above an initial stability threshold, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence relative to that threshold.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and tolerated learning rates, and Fixup's specified residual-network comparison. Transformer layer normalization is a different operation.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply because none of the supplied versions is tested. The original ReClor equality-based limits_scope label rests on a transcription error, and the T-Fixup failure does not challenge a claim about initialization under its stated conditions. The standard Spider 16-, 24- and 32-layer outcomes appear only as baselines in R12–R14, despite rows_left_out describing them as included rows. Table 7 also gives a different 8-layer standard result, 69.60 ± 0.40, from Table 5's 66.86 ± 0.16; these should remain distinct reported comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error from random initialization; CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100; corrupted or random labels; model size, early stopping and regularization comparisons.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus identity-shortcut convolutional networks and their training error; plain tanh networks; normalization-free residual training.
Activation-matched initializations, signal/gradient propagation measures, plain tanh networks with orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Learning rates above a stability threshold, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and divergence.
Batch normalization comparisons and the listed sigmoid, VGG, Inception, and Fixup settings.
